plain.text: Jacob lived in Canaan. His son Joseph, aged seventeen, tended the flocks with his brothers and brought their father a bad report about them. Israel loved Joseph more than his other sons, because he had been born in his old age, and he made him an ornate robe. His brothers hated him and could not speak a kind word to him. Joseph had a dream: they were binding sheaves of grain, and his brothers' sheaves bowed down to his. Then another: the sun, moon and eleven stars bowed down to him. His brothers hated him even more, and his father rebuked him, but kept the matter in mind.

Jacob sent Joseph to check on his brothers, who were grazing the flocks near Shechem. They saw him coming and plotted: "Here comes the dreamer! Let's kill him and see what becomes of his dreams." Reuben said, "Don't shed blood; throw him into this empty pit," planning to rescue him later. They stripped Joseph of his robe and threw him into the pit. As they ate, they saw a caravan of traders heading to Egypt. Judah said, "What will we gain if we kill our brother? Let's sell him." They sold Joseph for twenty pieces of silver, and he was taken to Egypt. Reuben returned to the pit and tore his clothes when he found Joseph gone.

The brothers dipped Joseph's robe in goat's blood and took it to their father. Jacob recognised it: "A wild animal has devoured him! Joseph has surely been torn to pieces!" He tore his clothes and mourned for many days, refusing to be comforted: "I will go down to the grave mourning for my son." Meanwhile the traders sold Joseph in Egypt to Potiphar, the captain of Pharaoh's guard.

summary.bigIdea: Favouritism and jealousy lead Joseph's brothers to sell him into slavery, and Jacob grieves the son he thinks is dead.
points: Jacob favours Joseph, giving him a special robe, and Joseph dreams of his family bowing to him.
His jealous brothers throw him in a pit and sell him to traders.
Jacob is told Joseph is dead and refuses to be comforted.
summary.reflection: Favouritism and jealousy did great harm in this family. Where might you need to guard against either?
